title: VFR Weather Minimums — 14 CFR 91.155 and Special VFR

questions.text: A pilot is flying VFR inside Class B airspace at 4,500 feet MSL. Visibility is 3 SM. Clouds are at the same altitude (scattered), with tops at 5,500 and bases at 4,200 feet — the pilot is flying between cloud layers. Is this legal under 14 CFR 91.155?

options.label: A
options.text: No — VFR flight BETWEEN cloud layers is prohibited in all airspace classes unless the pilot holds an instrument rating and operates under a VFR-on-top clearance issued by ATC with a modified ATC clearance from the ARTCC

options.label: B
options.text: No — VFR weather minimums in Class B require 3 SM visibility AND 500 feet below / 1,000 feet above / 2,000 horizontal cloud separation; flying at 4,500 between a 4,200-foot base and 5,500-foot top violates the 500-foot below and 1,000-foot above requirements

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — VFR weather minimums inside Class B airspace require only 3 SM visibility and to remain clear of clouds; there are no specific cloud distance requirements inside Class B; ATC provides IFR separation services eliminating the need for visual cloud buffers

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — any VFR aircraft in Class B may fly between layers as long as the pilot can maintain visual reference to the ground and the visibility through the cloud gaps is at least 3 SM; ATC's radar service provides the cloud separation function inside Class B

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.155 Table 1 establishes a unique weather minimum for Class B airspace: 3 SM flight visibility and CLEAR OF CLOUDS — no specific cloud distance requirement (no 500 below, no 1,000 above, no 2,000 horizontal). The rationale: inside Class B, ATC provides positive separation between all IFR and VFR aircraft using radar. The visual cloud separation buffer (500/1,000/2,000) exists in other airspace so VFR pilots can avoid encountering IFR aircraft emerging from clouds. Inside Class B, ATC manages all separation — the cloud buffer is redundant. If the pilot is clear of clouds (not in a cloud) and maintaining 3 SM visibility, the Class B weather minimum is met. Flying between layers with gaps is legal as long as the pilot is not inside a cloud. Applying the 500/1,000/2,000 cloud-separation standard to Class B is incorrect — that buffer belongs to other airspace classes. The claim that VFR flight between cloud layers is prohibited invents a rule that applies only to specific IFR procedures, not VFR operations in Class B. And requiring 'visual reference to the ground' adds a condition that does not exist in 91.155 for Class B.

questions.text: A commercial pilot (no instrument rating) requests and receives a Special VFR clearance to depart from a Class D airport at 10:00 PM local time. Visibility is 1.5 SM and ceilings are 700 feet. The flight will remain in the Class D surface area for departure. Is this operation legal under 14 CFR 91.157?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — the commercial pilot certificate supersedes the instrument rating requirement for night SVFR; commercial pilots are authorized to conduct night SVFR as a professional operation under the exception provisions of 14 CFR Part 61.133

options.label: B
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.157(b)(4) prohibits night Special VFR operations in Class D (and all controlled surface areas) unless the pilot holds an instrument rating; a commercial pilot without an instrument rating may not conduct night SVFR regardless of conditions or clearance type

options.label: C
options.text: No — Special VFR is only available during daylight hours to VFR pilots regardless of certificate grade; 14 CFR 91.157 specifically prohibits any SVFR clearance between official sunset and official sunrise for aircraft not operated under Parts 121 or 135

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — 14 CFR 91.157 Special VFR requires only 1 SM flight visibility at night; the pilot has 1.5 SM which exceeds the minimum, and the clearance was validly issued by ATC; no instrument rating is required for SVFR operations at or above 1 SM at night

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.157(b)(4) explicitly states that Special VFR may not be conducted at night (between official sunset and official sunrise) unless the aircraft is equipped for instrument flight and the pilot is instrument rated. This requirement applies to ALL pilots operating under Part 91, including commercial pilots without instrument ratings. A commercial certificate does not grant instrument privileges — those require completing the instrument rating checkride. The clearance being 'validly issued by ATC' does not cure the regulatory violation — ATC may issue an SVFR clearance believing the pilot is instrument rated; if they are not, the regulatory violation falls on the pilot. The claim that no instrument rating is needed for night SVFR is false. The claim that a commercial certificate creates an exception in Part 61.133 invents a provision that does not exist. And the position that SVFR is daylight-only for all VFR pilots over-restricts the rule — night SVFR IS available to instrument-rated pilots in IFR-equipped aircraft.

questions.text: A METAR for the destination airport shows: OVC008 1 3/4SM BR R28R/3600FT. The pilot needs 3 SM to land VFR. A flight school student says 'The RVR is 3600, that's well above 3 SM.' What is wrong with this interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing is wrong — RVR 3600 is shorthand for 3,600 statute miles of visibility on the approach end of Runway 28R; the METAR notation confirms the student's interpretation that conditions meet VFR minimums for landing

options.label: B
options.text: The student's interpretation is partially wrong — RVR 3600 represents 3,600 meters of visibility, which equals approximately 2.2 statute miles; conditions are still below the 3 SM VFR minimum, but the error magnitude is less severe than interpreting RVR in feet

options.label: C
options.text: The student confused RVR units — RVR 3600 means 3,600 FEET of runway visual range (approximately 0.68 statute miles), not 3,600 SM; at 0.68 SM forward visibility, the airport is significantly below the 3 SM required for VFR landing; the prevailing visibility '1 3/4SM' confirms conditions are below VFR minimums

options.label: D
options.text: The student's interpretation is wrong only for Class B airports — RVR values in Class B METARs are expressed in feet, but at Class C, D, and E airports, RVR in METARs is expressed in statute miles by FAA charting convention to avoid pilot confusion

questions.explanation: RVR (Runway Visual Range) in U.S. METARs is always expressed in feet — not statute miles, not meters. RVR 3600 means 3,600 feet of runway visual range. Converting: 3,600 feet ÷ 5,280 feet per mile ≈ 0.68 statute miles. The prevailing visibility from the METAR (1 3/4SM = 1.75 SM) is the legally operative number for VFR weather minimums — and 1.75 SM is far below the 3 SM VFR minimum. The 'OVC008' confirms a ceiling of 800 feet (800 feet OVC, which for VFR requires being 1,000 feet above clouds — the aircraft would need to be above 1,800 feet to satisfy cloud clearance, but the required ceiling for VFR below the clouds at 800 feet means the standard 3 SM / 500/1,000/2,000 minimums are not being met). Reading RVR 3600 as statute miles invents a conversion that produces the wrong result. Reading it as meters uses a unit that U.S. METAR RVR reporting does not use. And the claim that RVR units vary by airspace class invents a convention that does not exist.

questions.text: An untowered airport has a dashed magenta circle on the sectional chart. The current ASOS reports 2 SM visibility with a ceiling of OVC010. A VFR pilot is 5 miles out on final. Is the approach legal, and what airspace do the weather minimums apply to?

options.label: A
options.text: Legal — dashed magenta circles designate noise abatement zones, not airspace classes; the airport remains Class G from the surface; 2 SM visibility with a 1,000-foot ceiling is above the 1 SM clear-of-clouds Class G daytime surface minimum

options.label: B
options.text: Legal — any VFR approach at an untowered airport is legal as long as the pilot can maintain visual contact with the runway environment from 5 miles out; the airspace class of an untowered airport does not affect VFR approach legality

options.label: C
options.text: Legal — untowered airports are in Class G airspace by definition; Class G daytime minimums above 1,200 AGL are 1 SM and 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal; a ceiling of 1,000 feet (OVC010) and 2 SM visibility meets both standards for VFR approach

options.label: D
options.text: Not legal — the dashed magenta circle designates Class E from the surface; Class E weather minimums below 10,000 MSL require 3 SM visibility and 500 feet below / 1,000 feet above / 2,000 horizontal cloud separation; at 2 SM visibility, the pilot is below the Class E 3 SM minimum

questions.explanation: The dashed magenta boundary circle on a sectional chart designates a Class E surface extension — Class E airspace from the surface, created to protect IFR approach procedures at untowered airports. Although untowered (no communication requirement), this airspace is CONTROLLED airspace. Class E weather minimums below 10,000 MSL apply: 3 SM visibility and 500 below/1,000 above/2,000 horizontal cloud separation. At 2 SM visibility (below 3 SM required) with OVC010 (1,000-foot ceiling — technically adequate for 1,000 above, but the visibility violation alone makes it illegal), the approach is below VFR minimums. This is the most operationally critical trap of the airspace lessons: an untowered airport in Class E from the surface requires 3 SM VFR minimums even with no radio/ATC requirement. Classifying a dashed-magenta airport as Class G is incorrect. Identifying the dashed magenta circle as noise abatement instead of controlled airspace misreads the chart symbol. And treating airspace class as irrelevant to VFR approach legality is false.

questions.text: A fog bank moves across a Class D airport just after the tower opens at 6:00 AM. Visibility drops to 1.5 SM with an 800-foot ceiling. A VFR pilot wants to depart. The pilot calls the tower and ATC offers to 'help you get out if you want.' What is the regulatory status of a departure in these conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Legal only if the pilot specifically requests a Special VFR clearance from ATC — 14 CFR 91.157 allows VFR operations in Class D surface areas below standard VFR minimums with an ATC-issued SVFR clearance; conditions of 1.5 SM exceed the 1 SM SVFR minimum; the pilot must explicitly request SVFR — ATC cannot initiate it

options.label: B
options.text: Legal — ATC has radar services in Class D airspace; below VFR minimums, the tower can issue a 'low visibility departure clearance' equivalent to Special VFR under FAA Order JO 7110.65 without requiring an explicit SVFR request from the pilot

options.label: C
options.text: Legal — ATC's offer to 'help you get out' implies a de facto Special VFR clearance; ATIS and tower offering departure services constitutes an implicit SVFR authorization that meets the 91.157 request standard when conditions are 1.5 SM and 800 AGL

options.label: D
options.text: Illegal — once Class D weather drops below 3 SM or below ceiling minimums, no VFR operations including SVFR are legally available until conditions improve above standard VFR minimums; SVFR is only available in Class B, C, and E airspace, not Class D

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.157 authorizes Special VFR in controlled surface airspace (including Class D) when conditions are below standard VFR minimums but at or above 1 SM and clear of clouds. The critical requirement: the pilot must REQUEST Special VFR — ATC cannot unilaterally issue it. ATC saying 'I can help you get out' is not an SVFR clearance — it is likely ATC signaling that SVFR may be available, not issuing it. The pilot must say explicitly: 'Request Special VFR clearance to depart [airport] Class D surface area.' With 1.5 SM (above the 1 SM SVFR minimum) the conditions are legal for SVFR. This is a daytime operation with no instrument rating requirement for SVFR. Once clear of Class D, standard VFR minimums apply — at 1.5 SM and 800-foot ceiling, VFR flight outside the surface area likely still requires 3 SM in Class E. SVFR is only a surface area solution. Treating ATC's offer to 'help you get out' as an implicit SVFR authorization is false. Excluding Class D from SVFR availability is incorrect. And inventing a 'low visibility departure clearance' distinct from SVFR describes a procedure that does not exist.

questions.text: During an oral exam, the DPE asks: 'What are the VFR weather minimums in Class E airspace at 11,000 feet MSL during the day?' The applicant answers: '3 SM and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal.' Is the applicant correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — VFR weather minimums in Class E below 18,000 MSL are universally 3 SM and 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal regardless of altitude; the Class E above-10,000 minimum applies only to night operations above FL100

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — the Class E weather minimum change at 10,000 MSL only applies to Class E airspace in the contiguous United States; at 11,000 feet above mountain terrain or in non-contiguous states, the 3 SM standard applies because lower terrain density reduces collision risk

options.label: C
options.text: No — at 11,000 feet MSL the aircraft is approaching Class A airspace; the applicable minimums are the transition minimums for Class A approach corridors, which require 10 SM and a 2,000-foot ceiling buffer below FL180

options.label: D
options.text: No — at or above 10,000 feet MSL in Class E airspace, 14 CFR 91.155 requires 5 SM visibility and 1,000 feet below / 1,000 feet above / 1 SM horizontal cloud separation; at 11,000 MSL the pilot must apply the higher minimum set, not the below-10,000 standard

questions.explanation: The applicant failed a critical detail of 14 CFR 91.155. At or above 10,000 feet MSL in all controlled airspace (including Class E), the weather minimums increase to: 5 SM visibility, 1,000 feet below clouds, 1,000 feet above clouds, 1 SM horizontal cloud separation. At 11,000 feet MSL the applicant must apply 5 SM — not 3 SM. The rationale: aircraft cruising above 10,000 MSL typically fly at significantly higher true airspeeds, increasing closure rates with other traffic. More visibility provides adequate reaction time for see-and-avoid at these speeds. The applicant quoted the below-10,000 standard — a common memorization shortcut that fails above 10,000 feet. The claim that the 3 SM standard extends throughout Class E below FL180 is false. The claim that the 10,000-foot threshold varies geographically, applying only in the contiguous United States, invents a distinction that does not exist. And conflating Class E at 11,000 feet with Class A approach procedures misplaces the aircraft entirely.

questions.text: A VFR-only private pilot checks the destination METAR en route: 'KJAX 181755Z 17008KT 1 1/2SM BR OVC006 22/21 A2997 RMK AO2.' The pilot is 45 minutes out, flying in 4 SM in Class E at 4,500 feet, and thinks: 'IFR conditions ahead, but I can request Special VFR when I get there and duck under the clouds.' What is the safest assessment of this plan?

options.label: A
options.text: Sound plan — Special VFR at 1.5 SM exceeds the 1 SM SVFR minimum; requesting SVFR from Jacksonville Approach in advance gives the pilot legal authorization to land in instrument conditions as a VFR pilot, which is the intended use of 14 CFR 91.157

options.label: B
options.text: Flawed — SVFR allows VFR operations in CLASS D/E SURFACE AREAS at minimums of 1 SM clear of clouds; OVC006 (600-foot ceiling) means the pilot must fly at or below 600 feet to remain clear of clouds on approach; flying at 600 feet AGL in 1.5 SM visibility in fog toward an IFR airport is a high-risk operation that a VFR-only pilot should not plan; the correct action is to divert to VFR conditions rather than plan SVFR operations in sustained IFR weather

options.label: C
options.text: Flawed because Special VFR requires a daytime instrument rating — the pilot should instead request a VFR corridor through Jacksonville Center to transit the weather below the layer 500 feet above terrain, which is legally available to all Part 91 VFR pilots during the day under FAA Order JO 7110.65

options.label: D
options.text: Sound plan — Special VFR does not require the pilot to fly BELOW the ceiling; the SVFR clearance allows the pilot to fly ON TOP of the OVC layer at any altitude and descend through a gap in the overcast when within the Class D boundary; the 1.5 SM below the layer satisfies the SVFR visibility minimum

questions.explanation: This scenario is a textbook SVFR misuse trap. SVFR legally allows VFR operations at 1 SM and clear of clouds inside a surface area — but 'clear of clouds' at an OVC006 (600-foot ceiling) means operating at and below 600 feet AGL with a 1.5 SM forward visibility. For a VFR-only pilot with no instrument scan skills, 600 feet AGL in fog with 1.5 SM visibility near a major airport with IFR traffic on approach is a high-risk — and potentially fatal — environment. SVFR is a legal tool but a situational hazard when conditions are genuinely IFR. The professional response is diversion to VFR-condition airports, not a plan that routes an inexperienced VFR pilot through near-IFR conditions at low altitude. NTSB accident data: SVFR operations in actual IFR conditions consistently appear in VFR-into-IMC fatality reports. The plan to request SVFR in advance and land in instrument conditions is Invulnerability — rationalizing that SVFR resolves the hazard. Describing SVFR as an 'on top' operation that descends through a gap in the overcast is false. And the proposed VFR corridor to transit the weather is a procedure that does not exist.
questions.sjt_rationale: Get-There-Itis drives the SVFR plan — the pilot is problem-solving toward the destination rather than accepting that the destination is unavailable. SVFR is a legal mechanism, not a safety margin. The correct ADM is to recognize the environment is beyond safe VFR operation and divert.

questions.text: On a night cross-country at 8,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace, the forward visibility decreases to 4 SM. No clouds are visible. The pilot thinks: 'I can still see clearly forward and the minimum is 3 SM at night, so I'm legal.' What is the correct assessment?

options.label: A
options.text: Incorrect — at 8,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace, the pilot is above 1,200 AGL and the applicable standard is 3 SM visibility plus 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal cloud separation — not just 3 SM and clear; however, since no clouds are visible, the cloud separation requirement is effectively met; at 4 SM the visibility standard IS met; whether the pilot is inside the below-10,000 3 SM band (correct) or made a different error should be evaluated

options.label: B
options.text: Correct — night operations in Class E below 10,000 MSL have a minimum of 3 SM; at 4 SM the pilot exceeds the nighttime minimum and is legal; no clouds are visible so the clear-of-clouds requirement is also met

options.label: C
options.text: Incorrect — at 8,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace, since this altitude is above 10,000 MSL the higher minimums apply; the pilot is confusing MSL altitude with AGL altitude; 8,500 MSL may be more than 10,000 AGL in flat terrain

options.label: D
options.text: Correct only if VFR on top clearance is held — without an IFR clearance, a VFR pilot at 8,500 feet in reduced visibility must maintain 5 SM because the pilot is in the IFR en route structure above 3,000 AGL

questions.explanation: At 8,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace below 10,000 MSL: the applicable VFR weather minimum is 3 SM visibility, 500 feet below clouds, 1,000 feet above clouds, 2,000 feet horizontal cloud separation. The night classification does not raise the minimum at this altitude in Class E — the 3 SM/500/1,000/2,000 minimum applies whether day or night in controlled airspace below 10,000 MSL. The pilot's 4 SM visibility IS above the 3 SM minimum. With no clouds visible, cloud separation is not a concern. The pilot is technically legal at 4 SM. However, the pilot's reasoning is partially flawed — stating 'the minimum is 3 SM at night' is an oversimplification that ignores cloud separation. The complete analysis: 4 SM > 3 SM ✓, no clouds visible (infinite cloud separation) ✓. The flight is legal. The claim that 8,500 MSL may be above 10,000 AGL is incorrect — AGL altitude and MSL altitude are different only by terrain elevation; 8,500 MSL cannot be above 10,000 AGL. And the invented VFR-on-top requirement does not apply here.
questions.sjt_rationale: This question targets the common error of applying the Class G nighttime minimums to Class E operations. Class G night low-altitude = 3 SM clear. Class E below 10,000 = 3 SM with cloud separation (day or night). The pilot is safe in this scenario but for a partially correct reason — the teaching moment is precision in minimum application.
